purpose: Short original educational notes grounded in openly licensed pharmacology books. They support foundational learning only and are not clinical recommendations.
attribution_policy: Book-derived ideas are paraphrased rather than reproduced. Preserve each card's source references and attribution when adapting or redistributing notes.

cards.title: Pharmacokinetics: ADME
cards.summary: Pharmacokinetics describes how a substance moves through the body: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME). Route of administration and individual patient factors can affect exposure. A general ADME explanation does not establish an appropriate medicine or dose for a particular patient.
learning_points: ADME names four linked processes: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.
The same medicine can behave differently across routes and patient contexts.
Do not infer an individual dose from a foundational pharmacokinetics summary.

cards.title: Pharmacodynamics, efficacy, and dose-response
cards.summary: Pharmacodynamics concerns how a substance produces effects in the body, including interactions with biological targets. Potency, efficacy, dose-response, and therapeutic window describe different aspects of response; none can be used alone to select a treatment for an individual patient.
learning_points: Mechanism of action describes how a medicine produces a biological effect.
Potency and efficacy are related but distinct concepts.
The therapeutic window is a clinical concept that requires drug-specific evidence and patient context.

cards.title: Medication-history completeness
cards.summary: A medication history should distinguish prescribed medicines, nonprescription products, vitamins, herbal products, and other supplements. Where known, capture the exact product, strength/form, route, frequency, and reason for use; record unknown or not-reported facts explicitly rather than guessing. The clinician verifies the details before using them in a clinical decision.
learning_points: Don't collapse unknown, not asked, and none reported into the same value.
Record allergy reactions as reported and route them for clinician verification.
A list of medicines is context for review, not a complete interaction check.

cards.title: Adverse effects and unintended medication outcomes
cards.summary: A medicine can produce intended effects as well as unintended effects. Product labeling and appropriate clinical references separate warnings, contraindications, precautions, adverse reactions, and other information. A general educational note cannot establish whether a specific medicine is appropriate or safe for a person.
learning_points: Read the applicable product-specific label rather than relying on memory or a generic name alone.
Keep source version and date attached to label-derived information.
Do not equate a metadata match or absence of a surfaced warning with a safety conclusion.

cards.title: Antimicrobial therapy: learning concepts
cards.summary: Antimicrobial classes differ in their targets, spectrum, and safety considerations. Applying this background to a dental case requires the clinician's diagnosis and examination, the patient's circumstances, an applicable current guideline, and source-specific review. This card contains no medicine or dose recommendation.
learning_points: Class-level knowledge is not enough to select an antimicrobial for a patient.
Dental clinical guidelines define their own patient population and circumstances.
Do not infer an antibiotic indication or regimen from symptoms alone in this learning shelf.
